/ideal-weight/.sentence: Clinicians still use IBW equations “to calculate drug dosing, to estimate overweight and underweight statuses, and to calculate nutrient intakes,” Peterson and colleagues write.

Peterson and colleagues write that it “was originally defined as the weight associated with the greatest life expectancy at each height” and that “IBW equations are still being used by clinicians to calculate drug dosing, to estimate overweight and underweight statuses, and to calculate nutrient intakes.”

Pai and Paloucek concluded that “any one of these equations may be used to estimate IBW.” Robinson and colleagues found that estimates “obtained by the widely used empirical method probably contain only minor errors.” Peterson and colleagues point out that the equations give a single weight, where most clinicians favor a range.

/blog/bmi-and-health-risks/.sentence: Body Mass Index (BMI) is a screening tool for identifying potential health risks associated with weight.

J-curve relationship: both very low and very high BMI carry elevated all-cause mortality; the WHO healthy range (18.5–24.9) is the standard reference for lowest observed risk in most adult populations.
Cancer link: excess body weight is associated with at least 13 cancer types identified by IARC.
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide, and BMI is one of the most significant modifiable risk factors.
Excess body weight contributes to cardiovascular disease through multiple mechanisms including increased blood pressure, elevated cholesterol levels, chronic inflammation, and insulin resistance.
